source: HiRISE DTM + orthomosaic: USGS Mars 2020 TRN mosaics (DOI 10.5066/P9REJ9JN). Weather: Perseverance MEDA (PDS). Dust: Mastcam-Z tau (Lemmon). Positions: NASA/JPL Mars 2020 waypoints. Story items (lander, supplies, manual pages, visuals) are game fiction. See docs/DATA_SOURCES.md.

area.name: Jezero Crater: Octavia E. Butler Landing to the western delta front

sols.label: Sol 312: clear sky before the storm
sols.notes: Real MEDA + Mastcam-Z values. Normal Jezero day in northern winter (Ls ~153).

sols.label: Sol 1695: warmest afternoon in the sample
sols.notes: Real MEDA + Mastcam-Z values; hottest daytime air in the seasonal sample. No wind data this sol (MEDA wind sensor damaged on sol 313): windMS is the median daily mean wind of the 27 measured sols 55-313 (3.3 m/s), not a measurement.

sols.label: Sol 313: storm front arrives
sols.notes: Real. Pressure dips to 583 Pa, gusts to 12.5 m/s; the wind sensor is damaged this sol. No Mastcam-Z tau on sol 313: tau shown is sol 312's; sol 314 measured 0.64.

sols.label: Sol 316: storm peak
sols.notes: Real. Tau 1.38, the highest of this storm. No wind data after sol 313 (sensor damaged). No wind data this sol (MEDA wind sensor damaged on sol 313): windMS is the median daily mean wind of the 27 measured sols 55-313 (3.3 m/s), not a measurement.

sols.label: Sol 319: storm clearing
sols.notes: Real. Tau back down to ~0.44. No wind data this sol (MEDA wind sensor damaged on sol 313): windMS is the median daily mean wind of the 27 measured sols 55-313 (3.3 m/s), not a measurement.

technicalSpecs.backupPower: 28 kWh Lithium-Ion Solid-State Habitat Battery Bank

hardwareSites.name: Octavia E. Butler Landing
hardwareSites.history: Perseverance touchdown, Feb 18 2021 (sol 0). Position = first localisation, sol 13.
hardwareSites.scientificValue: Start of Perseverance's traverse; the rover studied the Máaz crater-floor rocks around here.
hardwareSites.clue: Rover wheel tracks lead South-East toward the Máaz formation.

hardwareSites.name: Wright Brothers Field (Ingenuity airfield)
hardwareSites.history: Ingenuity was dropped here around sol 43 and made the first powered flight on another planet on sol 58 (Apr 19 2021). Position = rover position on the deployment sol, within ~50 m.
hardwareSites.scientificValue: First powered, controlled flight on another planet.
hardwareSites.clue: Solar charging telemetry markers and historical aerial reconnaissance route log.

hardwareSites.name: Descent stage crash site
hardwareSites.history: The sky crane flew away after lowering the rover and crashed ~700 m north-west, leaving a V-shaped debris pattern.
hardwareSites.scientificValue: Seen from orbit by HiRISE the day after landing.
hardwareSites.clue: Salvageable structural titanium metal and high-temperature sensor wiring.

hardwareSites.name: Parachute and backshell
hardwareSites.history: The 21.5 m parachute and the backshell landed together ~1.1 km west-north-west. Ingenuity photographed the backshell standing upright on flight 26 (sol 418).
hardwareSites.scientificValue: Ingenuity's photos of the backshell helped engineers study how it survived entry.
hardwareSites.clue: Primary source for emergency shelter canopy fabric, insulation layers, and harness webbing.

hardwareSites.name: Heat shield impact
hardwareSites.history: Jettisoned during descent, the heat shield hit the ground ~1.5 km east-north-east.
hardwareSites.scientificValue: Its impact scar is visible in HiRISE images.
hardwareSites.clue: Rigid carbon-composite plating suitable for storm sled runners and shelter frames.

hardwareSites.name: Three Forks Sample Depot
hardwareSites.history: Ten sample tubes (9 rock/regolith/atmosphere + 1 witness tube) were dropped here between sol 653 and 690 (Dec 21 2022 - Jan 28 2023) as a backup cache for Mars Sample Return.
hardwareSites.scientificValue: The first sample depot on another planet.

rockFormations.name: Máaz formation (crater-floor lava)
rockFormations.associatedTarget: Roubion, Rochette (Guillaumes and Bellegarde abrasion patches)
rockFormations.mineralogy: Pyroxene and plagioclase feldspar with iron-titanium oxides, altered in places by water.
rockFormations.description: Iron-rich lava flows that cover the crater floor around the landing site, later altered by water. Source: SuperCam unit means, Wiens et al. 2022, 'Compositionally and density stratified igneous terrain in Jezero crater, Mars', Science Advances 8, eabo3399, Table 1 (open access, PMC9410274). Totals are below 100% because water and other light elements are not measured.
rockFormations.survivalApplication: Hard, stable ground for walking (design note).

rockFormations.name: Séítah formation (olivine cumulate)
rockFormations.associatedTarget: Brac, Issole (Garde and Dourbes abrasion patches)
rockFormations.mineralogy: Mostly olivine crystals (about 40% in the published norm) with pyroxene; olivine about Fo55-63.
rockFormations.description: Olivine crystals that settled to the bottom of a thick, slowly cooling body of magma. Much richer in magnesium than Máaz. Source: SuperCam unit means, Wiens et al. 2022, 'Compositionally and density stratified igneous terrain in Jezero crater, Mars', Science Advances 8, eabo3399, Table 1 (open access, PMC9410274). Totals are below 100% because water and other light elements are not measured.
rockFormations.survivalApplication: Rough, ridged ground with sand between the ridges: slow going (design note).

rockFormations.name: Western delta front
rockFormations.associatedTarget: Skinner Ridge, Wildcat Ridge, Amalik, Hidden Harbor
rockFormations.mineralogy: Fine-grained sandstone and mudstone with salts. SHERLOC found aromatic organic molecules in Wildcat Ridge.
rockFormations.description: Sediment carried by the river that once flowed into Lake Jezero. No bulk oxide values are given here: none were checked against a publication. Source for the organics: NASA/JPL, Sept 2022 (jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-perseverance-rover-investigates-geologically-rich-mars-terrain).
rockFormations.survivalApplication: The science target: see content.json scienceTarget.

rockFormations.name: Regolith (loose soil and dust)
rockFormations.associatedTarget: Observation Mountain regolith samples (Atmo Mountain, Crosswind Lake)
rockFormations.mineralogy: Basaltic sand with fine iron-oxide dust and salts, including perchlorates.

isruYields.hazardWarning: Heating perchlorate-bearing soil releases oxygen, HCl and chlorinated compounds that can contaminate the water. On Curiosity, chloromethanes came off mostly below 300 °C, together with the oxygen release that ended near 460 °C, so a 350 °C bake is already in this range (Leshin et al. 2013; Glavin et al. 2013, JGR Planets 118, 1955-1973). The 0.5 wt% perchlorate is the level Phoenix measured in polar soil (0.4-0.6 wt%, Hecht et al. 2009, Science 325, 64-67); Curiosity's Rocknest soil was comparable.

rockFormations.description: Loose soil that covers much of the crater floor. ISRU sources: Curiosity's SAM heated Gale soil (Rocknest, < 150 um) to ~835 °C and it released 1.5-3 wt% water in a broad peak centred near 300 °C (Leshin et al. 2013, Science 341, 1238937); the game uses 2 wt%, and 350 °C is a game value just past that peak. These are Gale and Phoenix measurements, not Jezero ones; Jezero's soil is similar wind-blown basaltic sand. No bulk oxide values are given.

fieldManualPages.title: Solar power in dust
fieldManualPages.sciencePrinciple: Dust in the air dims the direct beam of sunlight, but it scatters some light back down as a glowing sky, so panels still work under a dusty sky. At Jezero, overhead sun gives about 540 W/m² on flat ground at a normal dust level (tau 0.5) and about 430 W/m² at tau 1.5, close to the real January 2022 storm peak (tau 1.38). The bigger enemy is dust settling on the panel itself: output falls as a layer builds up. The Spirit and Opportunity rovers sometimes got their power back when wind gusts blew their panels clean.
fieldManualPages.source: NASA TM-103623, Appelbaum & Flood, 'Solar radiation on Mars: Update 1990'; Perseverance Mastcam-Z dust record (Lemmon). Values in public/data/sunlight.json and dust.json.
fieldManualPages.diagram: Sun ─► dust layer ─► direct beam (dims fast) + scattered sky light (stays) ─► panel ─► battery

fieldManualPages.title: Oxygen from a broken tank
fieldManualPages.sciencePrinciple: The AER-1 lander burned liquid oxygen (fiction). Liquid oxygen boils at -183 °C at Earth sea-level pressure, and one litre of it becomes roughly 800-860 litres of gas at room temperature and 1 atm. Even a little liquid left in a cracked tank is a lot of breathing gas. Warm it slowly through a coil, then let a regulator drop it to suit pressure (about 30 kPa of pure oxygen). Warming too fast builds dangerous pressure in a closed line.
fieldManualPages.source: Physical properties of oxygen (NIST Chemistry WebBook). The AER-1 lander and its oxygen tank are game fiction.
fieldManualPages.diagram: [Tank: liquid O2] ─► [Valve] ─► [Warming coil] ─► [Regulator ~30 kPa] ─► [Suit O2 port]

fieldManualPages.title: Finding a radio beacon
fieldManualPages.sciencePrinciple: Mars has no global magnetic field today, only patches of magnetised crust, so a compass will not point north. A loop antenna instead picks up a radio signal most weakly when its face points straight at the transmitter. Turn the loop until the signal fades to its quietest (the 'null'), and the beacon lies along that line. Take two bearings from different spots and the lines cross at the transmitter.
fieldManualPages.source: Mars Global Surveyor magnetometer results (Acuña et al., Science, 1999) for Mars' missing global field. Radio direction finding is standard radio practice. The rover beacon is game fiction.

fieldManualPages.title: Calling Earth through Perseverance
fieldManualPages.sciencePrinciple: Perseverance has three antennas. A UHF antenna (about 400 MHz) sends most of its data to orbiters passing overhead, at up to 2 megabits per second. Today these are NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Mars Odyssey and ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter (MAVEN, used early in the mission, was lost in 2025). Each pass lasts only about 10 to 17 minutes, so the rover can call out a few times a sol. The orbiters relay the data to NASA's Deep Space Network. A small X-band high-gain antenna can talk directly to Earth, but slowly, and is mostly used to receive each morning's commands. A low-gain antenna is the backup. The rover runs on a nuclear power source (about 110 W at the start of the mission), so it keeps working through dust storms. Radio takes about 3 to 22 minutes to cross between Mars and Earth, depending on where the planets are, so any reply comes back after a long wait.
fieldManualPages.source: NASA/JPL Mars 2020 landing press kit, Telecommunications (jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mars_2020/landing/mission/spacecraft/telecommunications); NASA Mars Relay Network (science.nasa.gov/mars/mars-relay-network); Mars Relay Network Handbook, JPL D-71874 Release 4 (2026). Connecting a survivor's radio to the rover is game fiction.
fieldManualPages.diagram: [Your radio] ─UHF─► [Perseverance] ─UHF─► [Orbiter: MRO / Odyssey / TGO] ─X-band─► [Deep Space Network, Earth]

fieldManualPages.title: Why your own breath is the danger
fieldManualPages.sciencePrinciple: Every breath out adds carbon dioxide to the suit, and only the scrubber removes it. Lithium hydroxide grabs CO2 in the reaction 2 LiOH + CO2 -> Li2CO3 + H2O, using about 1.09 kg of LiOH for every kg of CO2. When the canister is used up, CO2 in the suit air rises. Breathing harder cannot fix that, because your lungs cannot push CO2 below the level in the air you breathe in. Slow down to make less CO2, and swap the canister. Reference page: unlocks no build.
fieldManualPages.source: Reaction stoichiometry (molar masses LiOH 23.95 g/mol, CO2 44.01 g/mol); proposal §1.2 and §3.1.
fieldManualPages.diagram: Breath out ─► CO2 ─► [LiOH canister] ─► clean gas ─► breath in

daylightSky.description: Butterscotch / warm tan sky created by light scattering off suspended nanophase ferric oxide dust grains.
daylightSky.mieScattering: Fine dust grains (~1-2 micron) exhibit forward Mie scattering, giving the sky an illuminated yellowish-brown glow.

sunsetSky.description: Martian blue sunset. Forward scattering through the long atmospheric dust column allows blue wavelengths to penetrate while scattering away red wavelengths.
sunsetSky.timing: Visible 15-20 minutes before and after local Martian sunset.

lighting.shadowSharpness: Crisp and pitch-black under clear skies due to the absence of thick Rayleigh scattering in 1% atmosphere.
lighting.stormDarkness: During tau > 5.0 dust storms, direct illumination drops to <5% and daytime resembles twilight.
